label: Warfarin
message: Coumarin anticoagulants cause embryopathy (especially 6–12 weeks) and fetal bleeding. Switch to low-molecular-weight heparin under specialist advice.

label: ACE inhibitors
message: Fetal kidney damage and too little amniotic fluid, especially after the first trimester. Stop and change to labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa.
source: FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019); BNF

label: Angiotensin receptor blockers
message: Same fetal risks as ACE inhibitors. Stop and change to labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa.
source: FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019); BNF

label: Statins
message: Not recommended in pregnancy; stop until after breastfeeding unless a specialist advises otherwise.

label: Retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin)
message: Highly teratogenic. Must not be used in pregnancy.

label: Methotrexate
message: Teratogenic and abortifacient. Must not be used in an ongoing pregnancy.

label: Mycophenolate / leflunomide
message: Teratogenic. Specialist advice needed.

label: Valproate
message: Major malformations and developmental problems. Only if no alternative, under a neurologist, with high-dose folic acid.
source: MHRA / EMA valproate safety measures; BNF

label: Phenytoin / carbamazepine / phenobarbitone
message: Risk of malformations. Do not stop suddenly; neurologist review and folic acid 5 mg.

label: Lithium
message: Cardiac malformation risk and neonatal toxicity. Psychiatrist review; monitor levels.

label: Tetracyclines
message: Stain teeth and affect bone growth, especially after 15 weeks. Choose another antibiotic.

label: Fluoroquinolones
message: Usually avoided in pregnancy; use only if no safer alternative (e.g. cephalexin, nitrofurantoin before term).

label: Aminoglycosides
message: Risk of fetal hearing damage (streptomycin especially). Use only when clearly needed, with level monitoring.

label: Co-trimoxazole
message: Folate antagonist in the first trimester; risk of neonatal jaundice near term. Use only if needed, with folic acid.

label: Nitrofurantoin near term
message: Avoid at term (from 36 weeks): risk of neonatal haemolysis.

label: Chloramphenicol
message: Avoid near term: "grey baby" syndrome. (Eye drops are acceptable.)

label: NSAIDs from 20 weeks
message: From 20 weeks NSAIDs can reduce amniotic fluid and close the ductus arteriosus. Use paracetamol. (Low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention is different and is not included here.)
source: US FDA NSAID pregnancy warning (2020); BNF

label: NSAIDs before 20 weeks
message: Paracetamol is preferred. If an NSAID is needed, use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
source: US FDA NSAID pregnancy warning (2020); BNF

label: Carbimazole / methimazole in the first trimester
message: Linked with malformations in early pregnancy: propylthiouracil (PTU) is preferred up to 16 weeks, then switch back.
source: American Thyroid Association pregnancy guideline (2017); BNF

label: Misoprostol / mifepristone
message: Causes uterine contractions. Only under protocol – management of miscarriage, induction of labour or bleeding after delivery.

label: Ergometrine / methylergometrine before delivery
message: Causes sustained uterine contraction: only after the delivery of the baby (third stage / PPH).

label: Amiodarone
message: Fetal thyroid problems and growth restriction. Cardiologist advice needed.

label: Atenolol
message: Linked with fetal growth restriction. Labetalol or nifedipine are usually preferred.
source: FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019); NICE NG133

label: Benzodiazepines
message: Near term: floppy baby and withdrawal. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.

label: Codeine / tramadol
message: Regular use near term causes neonatal withdrawal and breathing problems.

label: Clomiphene / letrozole
message: Not for use once pregnant: stop the fertility treatment.

label: Danazol / testosterone
message: Virilisation of a female fetus.

label: Finasteride / dutasteride
message: Affects male fetal development.

label: Thalidomide
message: Severe limb and organ malformations. Must not be used in pregnancy.

label: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever)
message: Live vaccines are not given in pregnancy. Tetanus-diphtheria (Td), influenza and Tdap are safe.

label: High-dose vitamin A
message: Doses above 10,000 IU a day are teratogenic. Check the dose.

label: Iron and calcium together
message: Calcium reduces iron absorption. Advise taking them at least 2 hours apart (e.g. iron in the morning, calcium at night).
source: MoHFW India Anemia Mukt Bharat / IFA and calcium supplementation guidelines (2018)

label: Thyroxine with iron or calcium
message: Iron and calcium reduce thyroxine absorption. Thyroxine on an empty stomach, at least 4 hours apart from iron and calcium.
source: American Thyroid Association pregnancy guideline (2017); BNF

label: Nifedipine with magnesium sulphate
message: Watch for low blood pressure and muscle weakness; monitor BP, reflexes and breathing.
source: FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019); BNF

label: Low-dose aspirin with an NSAID
message: Higher bleeding risk, and ibuprofen can reduce aspirin's effect. Prefer paracetamol for pain.

label: Codeine
message: Some mothers turn codeine into morphine very quickly: the baby can become drowsy and stop breathing. Use paracetamol or ibuprofen.
source: MHRA / EMA codeine safety advice (2013); BNF; LactMed

label: Tramadol
message: Lowest dose for the shortest time. Watch the baby for drowsiness, poor feeding and slow breathing. (The US FDA advises against it while breastfeeding.)
source: US FDA drug safety communication (2017); LactMed; BNF

label: Bromocriptine / cabergoline
message: Stops milk production. Only when stopping lactation is intended.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Ergometrine / methylergometrine (repeated doses)
message: A single dose after delivery is acceptable. Repeated doses can reduce the milk supply and may affect the baby.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Combined contraceptive pill (with oestrogen)
message: Oestrogen reduces the milk supply: not in the first 6 weeks after delivery, and preferably not until 6 months while she is mainly breastfeeding. Progestogen-only methods, a copper IUCD or condoms are preferred.
source: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use (5th edition, 2015); BNF

label: Amiodarone
message: Passes into milk in large amounts; the iodine can cause hypothyroidism in the baby.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Lithium
message: Passes into milk; risk of toxicity in the baby. Only with psychiatrist advice and monitoring of the baby.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Methotrexate / cyclophosphamide
message: Cytotoxic: breastfeeding should stop during treatment. Specialist advice needed.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin)
message: Not to be used while breastfeeding.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Statins
message: Manufacturers advise against use while breastfeeding; treatment can usually wait.

label: Tetracyclines
message: A short course (up to 3 weeks) is acceptable. Avoid long or repeated courses: possible staining of the baby’s teeth.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Fluoroquinolones
message: Use only if there is no safer alternative. Watch the baby for diarrhoea and thrush.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Chloramphenicol
message: Avoid by mouth or injection: possible bone-marrow effects in the baby. (Eye drops are acceptable.)
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Metronidazole / tinidazole
message: Ordinary doses are acceptable (the milk may taste bitter). After a single 2 g dose, express and discard the milk for 12 to 24 hours (tinidazole: 3 days).
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Nitrofurantoin
message: Avoid if the baby is under 1 month old, jaundiced or has G6PD deficiency: risk of haemolysis.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Co-trimoxazole / sulfonamides
message: Avoid if the baby is under 1 month old, preterm, jaundiced or has G6PD deficiency: risk of kernicterus and haemolysis.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Aspirin
message: Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg a day) is acceptable. Avoid pain-relief doses: possible risk of Reye’s syndrome in the baby. Use paracetamol or ibuprofen.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Benzodiazepines
message: Can make the baby drowsy and feed poorly, especially with repeated doses. Lowest dose for the shortest time.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Phenobarbitone / primidone
message: Can make the baby drowsy. Do not stop suddenly; neurologist review.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Atenolol
message: Builds up in milk: slow heart rate and low blood sugar in the baby have been reported, more so in a preterm baby or one under 3 months. Labetalol, nifedipine or enalapril are preferred.

label: Carbimazole / methimazole
message: Passes into milk: use the lowest effective dose and check the baby’s thyroid function.
source: BNF (breast-feeding); American Thyroid Association pregnancy and postpartum guideline (2017)

label: Pseudoephedrine (decongestants)
message: Can reduce the milk supply, even after a single dose.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Povidone-iodine (repeated use)
message: Iodine is absorbed and concentrated in milk: repeated use (for example vaginal pessaries) can affect the baby’s thyroid.
source: LactMed (US National Library of Medicine); BNF (breast-feeding)

label: Ceftriaxone in the first 28 days
message: Do not use in a jaundiced, preterm or acidotic baby (it displaces bilirubin), and never with calcium-containing infusions. Cefotaxime is preferred.
source: BNF for Children; WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013)

label: Co-trimoxazole / sulfonamides under 6 weeks
message: Risk of kernicterus, more so in a jaundiced baby. Not under 6 weeks of age (except for pneumocystis, under specialist advice).

label: Chloramphenicol in the first 28 days
message: By mouth or injection: “grey baby” syndrome. Only if there is no alternative, with blood-level monitoring. (Eye drops and ointment are acceptable.)

label: Nitrofurantoin under 3 months
message: Risk of haemolysis. Not under 3 months of age.

label: Vitamin K3 (menadione)
message: Causes haemolysis and jaundice in newborns. Use vitamin K1 (phytomenadione).
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Aspirin
message: Risk of Reye’s syndrome in children under 16. Only under specialist advice (for example Kawasaki disease).

label: Codeine / tramadol
message: Not for children under 12: risk of slow or stopped breathing.
source: MHRA / EMA codeine safety advice (2013); US FDA drug safety communication (2017)

label: Tetracyclines
message: Stain the teeth and affect bone growth. Not for young children.

label: Fluoroquinolones
message: Usually avoided in children (joint and tendon effects). Only if there is no safer alternative.

label: Ibuprofen under 3 months
message: Not recommended under 3 months of age or under 5 kg. Paracetamol is preferred.

label: Mefenamic acid under 6 months
message: Not recommended under 6 months of age. Paracetamol is preferred.

label: Promethazine
message: Not for children under 2 years: risk of slow or stopped breathing.
source: US FDA boxed warning (children under 2 years); BNF for Children

label: Cough and cold medicines
message: Not for young children: no proven benefit and reports of serious harm.
source: MHRA cough and cold medicines advice (2009)

label: Loperamide
message: Not for young children: risk of paralytic ileus. Diarrhoea is treated with ORS and zinc.
source: BNF for Children; WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013)

label: Metoclopramide under 1 year
message: Not under 1 year of age: risk of movement disorders.
source: EMA metoclopramide review (2013); BNF for Children

label: Domperidone
message: No longer recommended for nausea and vomiting in children under 12 years or under 35 kg.

label: Paracetamol
message: Less for an adult under 50 kg or with liver disease.

label: Ibuprofen
message: Usual dose 300–400 mg three or four times a day.

label: Diclofenac
message: By any route.

label: Tranexamic acid
message: Heavy periods: 1 g three times a day for up to 4 days.

label: Ondansetron
message: The limit is for one dose into a vein: higher doses lengthen the QT interval. By mouth the usual dose is 4 to 8 mg, two or three times a day.

label: Metoclopramide
message: For up to 5 days.

label: Domperidone
message: For up to 7 days.

label: Labetalol (by mouth)
message: In 2 to 4 divided doses.
source: BNF; FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019)

label: Nifedipine
message: Extended-release tablets (the BNF gives 90 mg a day). Short-acting capsules for severe hypertension only under protocol.
source: FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019); ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 (2020); BNF

label: Methyldopa
source: BNF; FOGSI GCPR Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (2019)

label: Metformin
message: The manufacturer’s label allows up to 3 g a day in divided doses.

label: Clomifene
message: For 5 days in a cycle. Higher doses only under specialist care.

label: Letrozole (ovulation induction)
message: For 5 days in a cycle (off-label use).
source: ACOG Practice Bulletin 194, Polycystic ovary syndrome (2018)

label: Iron sucrose (IV)
message: Not more than 3 times a week; the total dose is worked out from her weight and haemoglobin.

label: Ferric carboxymaltose (IV)
message: Not more than 20 mg/kg in one dose, and not more than 1000 mg in a week.

label: Betamethasone
message: Antenatal steroid course: 12 mg, two doses 24 hours apart.
source: WHO recommendations on antenatal corticosteroids (2022); RCOG Green-top Guideline 74

label: Carboprost
message: Every 15 minutes at the soonest; at most 8 doses (2 mg).
source: WHO Managing complications in pregnancy and childbirth (2017); manufacturer’s label

label: Methylergometrine
message: At most 5 doses (1 mg) in 24 hours. Not in high blood pressure.
source: WHO Managing complications in pregnancy and childbirth (2017); manufacturer’s label

label: Paracetamol (baby)
message: By mouth: usual dose 10–15 mg/kg (a first dose of 20 mg/kg). Preterm, under 32 weeks corrected age: at most 30 mg/kg a day. By injection the doses are lower – see the BNF for Children.
source: BNF for Children; WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013)

label: Amoxicillin (baby, by mouth)
message: Young infants: 50 mg/kg twice a day. The BNF for Children allows more in severe infection.
source: WHO guideline: possible serious bacterial infection in young infants (2015); BNF for Children

label: Ampicillin (baby, first week of life)
message: First week of life: 50 mg/kg every 12 hours. In meningitis up to 100 mg/kg a dose – this caution is then expected.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Ampicillin (baby)
message: After the first week of life: every 8 hours, then every 6 hours. Up to 100 mg/kg a dose in meningitis.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Gentamicin (baby, first week of life)
message: First week of life: 5 mg/kg once a day; 3 mg/kg for a low-birth-weight baby.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Gentamicin (baby)
message: Once a day, after the first week of life.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Amikacin (baby)
message: Once a day.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Cefotaxime (baby, first week of life)
message: First week of life: every 12 hours (BNF for Children). The WHO Pocket book gives 50 mg/kg every 8 hours for a term baby – this caution is then expected.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Cefotaxime (baby)
message: After the first week of life: every 6 to 8 hours.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children

label: Phenobarbitone (baby)
message: Loading dose 20 mg/kg; further doses of 10 mg/kg, up to 40 mg/kg in all, raise this caution. Maintenance is about 5 mg/kg a day – the check cannot tell a maintenance dose from a loading dose.
source: WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children (2013); BNF for Children
